title: 1.1 Course Introduction
text:
What is “Data Science”?


“Data science combines math and statistics, specialized programming, advanced analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning with specific subject matter expertise to uncover actionable insights hidden in an organization’s data. These insights can be used to guide decision making and strategic planning.”
– IBM Cloud Education

title: 1.1 Course Introduction

“The ability to take data — to be able to understand it, to process it, to extract value from it, to visualize it, to communicate it — that’s going to be a hugely important skill in the next decades.”
– Hal Varian, chief economist at Google and UC Berkeley Professor of Information Sciences, Business, and Economics

title: 1.1 Course Introduction

What is “Data Science”?


“Data Science draws upon multiple disciplines to develop or apply computational and analytic methods to responsibly explore data and discover actionable insights and accelerate translation into implementation with real-world evidence.”
– University of Pittsburgh Data Science Task Force

title: 1.1 Course Introduction
text:
What is “Data Science”?


“Data Science is about drawing useful conclusions from large and diverse data sets through exploration, prediction, and inference.
Exploration involves identifying patterns in information.
Prediction involves using information we know to make informed guesses about values we wish we knew.
Inference involves quantifying our degree of certainty: will the patterns that we found in our data also appear in new observations? How accurate are our predictions?
Our primary tools for exploration are visualizations and descriptive statistics, for prediction are machine learning and optimization, and for inference are statistical tests and models.”
– Computational and Inferential Thinking

title: 1.1 Course Introduction
text:
Class Definition

Data science is the study of the collection, storage, analysis, and visualization/communication of recorded information.

Collection: how observed events and/or characteristics are recorded in ways that can be explored sometime in the future.
Storage: How information is efficiently stored for later recall.
Analysis: How information is processed and organized in order to predict outcomes, or make official statements, about recorded information.
Visualization/Communication: How information is presented in order to communicate a message motivated by recorded information.

title: Homework 1 - STAT 1080
text:
Part b (5 points)
Now, write an equivalent expression that calculates the mean, without using the mean() function. For this, we will rely on the general definition of a mean. Let \(X\) represent a vector of values, with the individual elements of the vector denoted as \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) respectively. Under this definition we can calculate the sample mean of \(X\) (called \(\bar{x}\)) as
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n}.\] ::: {.callout-note collapse=true} ### Math Notation for the mean
Let’s break the math down a bit.

\(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean of the vector \(X\), which has values – \(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n\). We use capital letters for vectors and lower-case values for observations.
\(\sum_{i=1}^n\) says we’re going to take the sum of \(n\) things, which are indexed (\(i\) is the index of \(x_i\)) from 1 to \(n\).
We then divide the sum of the \(x_i\) (that is, the sum over \(X\)) by the length of \(X\), which is \(n\).

:::
Restated in plain English, I am taking the sum of all the elements of the vector, and then dividing by the length of the vector (or, if I am ignoring NAs, the sum of instances for which !is.na() evaluates to TRUE).






NoteMissing Observations





Sometimes, we can have missing observations, which are denoted by NA. If there are missing observations, we should exclude the missing observations from the sum (in the numerator/on the top of the fraction), and then exclude the missing observations from the number of total observations.
In R, we can exclude NAs from most functions by using fn(..., na.rm = T), where fn is the function name and ... are the other arguments.



Using this definition, re-calculate the mean added sugar content of the cereals without using the mean() function in R. You may consider using functions in R that match one, or both, of the bolded words in the equation description. Remember that, should you have to remove any missing values as part of your calculation, you need to account for that in your estimation of the vector length. Assign this to the variable name sugar_mean_2 and use the last line of code to make sure that this calculation of the mean exactly matches the previous calculation.

##   summarize(tmean = #...#) |>
##   pull(tmean)

## all.equal(sugar_mean_2, hw1_sol$sugar_mean_1)

title: Activity: Bread Programming
text:
Introduction
This assignment introduces some of the principles of object oriented programming using the metaphor of a peanut (or almond) butter and jelly sandwich. The goal of this assignment is to create a set of ordered commands that properly use the necessary objects to make a sandwich. Each object has a series of actions. Some actions are active (i.e. the object does the action) and some are passive (i.e. the object receives the action). Below is a list of the objects and the actions associated with sandwich creation.



Object
Active Actions
Passive Actions




Bag
None
Open; Close


Bread_Slice
Combine
Take; Place Left; Place Right


Jar
None
Open; Close


Knife
Load; Spread
Take; Set Down


Peanut_Butter
None
None


Jam
None
None



Note that we sometimes have the same object with two different names. For example, the “Peanut Butter Jar” and the “Jam Jar” are both “Jar” objects, but are referred to as separate things in the the list of commands. You may alternatively label them as “Jar 1” and “Jar 2”. The same goes for knives - you may not use the same knife for the PB and the J, because you’re not a monster.


Task
You must write a set of commands that walks someone through the process of making a PB & J sandwich. Your instructions must be exact as the builder of the sandwich cannot guess what you meant if any command is imprecise. You should each command should be exactly one action and there should be only one command on each line. You will work in groups of 3-4 to type a set of commands that will be used in real time. We will experiment with a few different group scripts during the class period. Once you have completed your sandwich script (meaning you have created what you believe is a comprehensive set of instructions for assembling the sandwich), you will take the Canvas quiz associated with this assignment.
The list of possible commands are below. Each jar must be named according to the number given on the knife or jar.

load knife with jam/butter (must specify knife number)
combine bread_slice (must name two bread slices)
Open/close bag/jar (must specify jar number and bag type)
take/set knife/bread_slice (can set left or right, or on/in another object)
spread jam/butter with knife on bread_slice (must specify knife and bread slice number)

Office hours
Office hours are available by appointment at this link. In general, office hours will be via Zoom - this allows me to offer more availability, and doesn’t require you to come to East campus to visit my office.
If you’d prefer to meet in person, try to schedule your appointment on Monday or Wednesday, and mention in the request that you want an in-person meeting. I will let you know if that’s feasible given my schedule for the day.

title: Course support
text:
Email
Please only use email for questions about personal matters that may not be appropriate for the public course forum (e.g., illness, grades, accommodations, etc.). In these cases, please add “STAT349” to the subject line, so that I can prioritize your email.
Assignment and content related questions should be asked in the relevant discussion board on Canvas.

title: Course support
text:
Academic support
There are times you may need help with the class that is beyond what can be provided by the teaching team. In those instances, I encourage you to visit the Center for Academic Success and Transition (CAST). CAST offers free services to all students.
Students have access to peer tutoring, academic coaching, and academic success workshops.

title: Course support
text:
Mental health and wellness
Your mental health and wellness extremely important, and the university offers resources to support students in managing daily stress and self-care. UNL offers several resources for students to manage stress, seek help with well-being, and access crisis and long-term care.

Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS), 402-472-7450
Center for Advocacy, Response, & Education (CARE), 402-472-3553 – resources for victims/survivors of interpersonal violence.
Services for Students with Disabilities (SSD), ssd@unl.edu or 402-472-3787 – resources for students experiencing short or long-term disabilities that affect the campus or educational experience.

title: Stat 1080 Syllabus
text:
1.2 Software
This course will involve programming in the R statistical programming language. R is a free and open-source language: a large community of people contribute to R without pay, and a larger community of people use R without having to pay for it. The language is particularly good at data wrangling and data visualization. In addition, the community has developed a large number of extra packages to augment the language, making it easy to read in, visualize, and model new and different types of data.
Some of these packages also allow you to run other programming languages, such as Python, within R. This makes R a good, but not the only, platform to begin to learn programming essentials in a software actively used by professionals in the workforce.
You must have either a working laptop or a chromebook during each class period. It will not be feasible to complete the programming assignments in this class on your phones.
Laptop setup: You will need

a current version of R (4.5.0 or later) installed
RStudio (2026.1.0 or later) installed
Quarto (1.10.0 or later) installed
Updated versions of all software packages (as of the first week of class)

Chromebook setup: There is a browser based version of R and RStudio that you will be expected to access. Access is free for the first 25 compute hours. However, if your compute hours exceed the free allotment, you may need to upgrade to a student account for $5/month. I recommend waiting to upgrade your account until you absolutely have to.
If your laptop breaks unexpectedly during the semester, contact the IT service desk for help. Loaner laptops may be available for short or long term use; you can then use the chromebook instructions to access RStudio in a browser until your laptop is fixed.

3.4.2 Extenuating Circumstances

You have chronic migraines and have missed 8 classes this semester.

title: Stat 1080 Syllabus
text:
3.10 Evaluation and Academic Integrity
Students are expected to adhere to guidelines concerning academic dishonesty outlined in Article VI University Regulations Regarding Academic Integrity. In this course, academic dishonesty includes failure to disclose use of AI (depending on sources of aid beyond those permitted), as well as more traditional examples of academic dishonesty.
The policies detailed below stand in addition to university policies.
Summary: I may, at my discretion, give students an oral exam on their submitted assignment to replace the graded assignment itself. That is, if you submitted it, you should be able to defend, discuss, and justify your work.ss

3.10.1 Evaluation Criteria
In every assignment, discussion, and written component of this class, you are expected to demonstrate that you are intellectually engaging with the material. I will evaluate you based on this engagement, which means that technically correct but low effort answers which do not demonstrate engagement or understanding will receive no credit.
When you answer questions in this class, your goal is to show that you either understand the material or are actively engaging with it. If you did not achieve this goal, then your answer is incomplete, regardless of whether or not it is technically correct. This is not to encourage you to add unnecessary complexity to your answer - simple, elegant solutions are always preferable to unwieldy, complex solutions that accomplish the same task.
Grammar and spelling are important, as is your ability to communicate technical information clearly in a written format; both of these criteria will be used in addition to assignment-specific rubrics to evaluate your work.


3.10.2 Code
You must be able to explain how the logic works for any code you turn in. This means that code you obtained from e.g. StackOverflow is fine to use if you can explain it and modify it for the purposes of this class, but if you cannot explain your code you will not get credit for the assignment. This is in line with what is generally considered acceptable behavior in programming - reuse is fine (subject to the code’s license) but you must be able to fully explain and modify any code you did not write yourself. You should also provide a link to the source of your code (or even the logic behind your code) - this is useful both for my information and for future you, in addition to being a good way to give attribution to the original author.


3.10.3 Oral Exam Policy
With the proliferation of AI large language models, I reserve the right to replace homework grades with grades based on an oral discussion of your submissions. If you cannot explain the logic behind your submission, how you came to the approach you used, and identify the tradeoffs behind decisions you made, then you will not receive credit. LLMs can be a useful tool, but this course’s objectives are to develop your understanding of data science, not your ability to use LLMs. Fundamentally, you need to understand concepts and apply methodology in order to use data effectively; generative AI solutions may hamper both of these goals if you rely on them too much.


3.10.4 Generative AI
It may be useful to leverage AI tools to ensure that your work conforms to grammar and style guidelines, but I very highly discourage the use of generative AI to actually write content or to execute a data analysis. I highly prefer your writing and thought process, even with some mistakes, to the bland content generated by most LLMs.
Any use of generative AI must be disclosed in an appendix to your submission - this includes brainstorming, editing, using AI as spell-check/grammar-check, and so on. You must document the following:

the version of the generative AI used (e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT 5.2, Copilot GPT-5 chat)
the full sequence of prompts and responses
any additional inputs you provided to the AI system (documents, images, etc.)
a “diff” between the AI responses and your submission, showing exactly what was generated by the AI system and what you changed. If you are using quarto, you can use the diff command line tool to get this (you may have to fix headers) after you’ve pasted the AI text into its own document.

title: Bias and Ethics
text:
The following code shows you how to obtain a relationship between two variables in a dataset internal to R. You will learn how to write this code yourself eventually, but today the code is just provided you you. All you need to do is click the little green arrow in the upper right corner of each grey box to run the code.

# Convert table to dataframe
ucb_df <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)

# Aggregate across departments
agg_df <- ucb_df |>
  group_by(Gender, Admit) |>
  summarise(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Prop = Freq / sum(Freq))

# Plot: proportion admitted by gender
ggplot(agg_df, aes(x = Gender, y = Prop, fill = Admit)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "UC Berkeley Graduate Admissions (1973)",
    y = "Proportion within Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    fill = "Admission Status"
  )








The above plot shows you that women are more likely to be rejected from University of California - Berkely (UCB) than men. Please take some time to ensure that you understand how the plot backs up that claim.


Suppose an uninformed viewer of this plot makes the claim “we should discourage women from applying to UCB since there applications are less competitive than male applicants.”

STOP here Go to Canvas Answer Quiz question 1: why this claim is problematic
Resume after quiz question 1 is answered.

Now, consider the plot created by the code below

dept_df <- ucb_df |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender, Admit) |>
  summarise(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  mutate(Total = sum(Freq),
         Rate = Freq / Total) |>
  filter(Admit == "Admitted")

# Plot admission rates by department and gender
ggplot(dept_df, aes(x = Dept, y = Rate, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "UC Berkeley Graduate Admissions (1973)",
    subtitle = "Admission rate by Department and Gender",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Admission Rate",
    fill = "Gender"
  )








What we see now is that the overall effect we observed has been reversed: women appear to be admitted at the same or higher rate in each individual department.



Before how this happened, another uninformed reader says “we should force the male and female application rates to be exactly the same in order to ensure fairness.”

STOP here Go to Canvas Answer Quiz question 2: why this claim is problematic
Resume after quiz question 2 is answered.

The above plot shows you that women are more likely to be rejected from University of California - Berkely (UCB) than men. Please take some time to ensure that you understand how the plot backs up that claim.


Suppose an uninformed viewer of this plot makes the claim “we should discourage women from applying to UCB since there applications are less competitive than male applicants.”

STOP here Go to Canvas Answer Quiz question 1: why this claim is problematic
Resume after quiz question 1 is answered.

Now, consider the plot created by the code below

dept_df <- ucb_df |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender, Admit) |>
  summarise(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  mutate(Total = sum(Freq),
         Rate = Freq / Total) |>
  filter(Admit == "Admitted")

# Plot admission rates by department and gender
ggplot(dept_df, aes(x = Dept, y = Rate, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "UC Berkeley Graduate Admissions (1973)",
    subtitle = "Admission rate by Department and Gender",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Admission Rate",
    fill = "Gender"
  )








What we see now is that the overall effect we observed has been reversed: women appear to be admitted at the same or higher rate in each individual department.



Before how this happened, another uninformed reader says “we should force the male and female application rates to be exactly the same in order to ensure fairness.”

STOP here Go to Canvas Answer Quiz question 2: why this claim is problematic
Resume after quiz question 2 is answered.

title: Bias and Ethics
text:
Putting it all together
The final code helps to demystify the issue:

# Total applications by department and gender
apps_df <- ucb_df |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  summarise(Applications = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  mutate(Share = Applications / sum(Applications))

# Plot 1: raw counts of applications
ggplot(apps_df, aes(x = Dept, y = Applications, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Applications by Department and Gender",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Number of Applications",
    fill = "Gender"
  )







# Plot 2: proportion of each gender's applications going to each department
ggplot(apps_df, aes(x = Dept, y = Share, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Application Share by Department",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Proportion of Applications",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) 







# Plot 3: raw numbers of each gender's applications going to each department
ggplot(ucb_df, aes(x = Gender, weight = Freq, fill = Dept)) + geom_bar(position = "stack") +
  labs(
    title = "Applications by Gender and Department",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of Applications",
    fill = "Department"
  ) 








Thus, the answer to “Simpson’s Paradox” is this: the reason that women appear to be admitted at a lower rate than men is because women were disproportionately more likely to apply to more selective departments. More importantly, this assignment reminded you that not all decisions can be effectively or ethically made with data alone.

Industry uses R for prototyping, Python/C for production

Easy to write bad/hard-to-maintain code
This is true in almost every language
Different conventions than C/Python/Java
Counting from 1, 2, 3, … rather than 0, 1, 2, …
